label: Postgres: Query
description: Run SQL against Postgres and get the rows back. Parameters are the node's own inline-declared input ports, read by name: `PostgresExecuteQuery(user_id: String) { query: "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $user_id" }`. Binding: a string as the text of the placeholder's type (so `$when::timestamptz`, a uuid column or `$amount::numeric` parse it like a quoted literal), a boolean as bool, a number to whatever numeric column it meets, null anywhere, an object or list as jsonb (`$params::jsonb->>'id'`). Where Postgres cannot infer a parameter's type (inside `jsonb_build_object(...)`, `$x IS NULL`, bare `SELECT $x`) it refuses with "could not determine data type of parameter": cast it (`$x::text`). A port used twice is ONE parameter with one type, so `'...' || $id` makes `id` text and a uuid or integer comparison on it then fails; use a separate port. Several statements form a script: with `$name` parameters they run in one transaction, each with the ports it names; without any, all but the last run whole (transaction control and utility statements work) and the last runs alone. The last statement's rows come back. Declare output ports (`-> (name: String)`) to read the first row's columns; a nullable column is typed `T | Null` (`List[Dict[String, JsonDict | Null]]`), since `JsonDict` alone refuses null. To fail on purpose, define once in the schema `CREATE FUNCTION fail(msg text) RETURNS void LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ BEGIN RAISE EXCEPTION '%', msg; END $$;` and call `SELECT fail('no such publication') WHERE NOT EXISTS (...)` (a `$port` inside a `DO` body is plain text, not a parameter). A data-modifying CTE (`WITH ins AS (INSERT ... RETURNING *) SELECT ...`) is invisible to the rest of its statement: read from `ins`, not the table. Unreachable database, broken constraint, `fail(..)` or missing privilege: catchable by `error`. An SQL mistake (syntax, unknown table or column, positional `$1`): always fails the run.

inputs.name: account
inputs.description: Wire a PostgresAccess, or a PostgresDatabase's access output.

inputs.name: query
inputs.label: SQL
inputs.description: The SQL; each `$name` reads the inline-declared input port of that name.

outputs.name: rows
outputs.description: Answered rows keyed by column (the last statement's, for a script).

outputs.name: count
outputs.description: Rows RETURNED (length of `rows`), not rows changed: a plain INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE gives 0; add `RETURNING id` to count them. A column named `count` cannot use this port: alias it (`count(*) as total`) and declare that port.

then.message: '{id}' aliases a column to `count` or `rows`, which are this node's own outputs (how many rows came back, and the rows themselves). A column of that name has nowhere to go: reading the port gives you what the node puts there. Alias it to something else in the SQL, `count(*) as total`, and declare a port for that name.

'{id}' wires `count`, but its statement answers no rows: `count` is how many rows came BACK, not how many a write changed, so it would be 0 on a write that worked perfectly and anything gated on it would never fire. Add `RETURNING id` (or whichever column) to the statement, and `count` becomes the number of rows it touched.
